item: Hagen 2018 Et nyt tempelarkiv fra Det Nye Rige
citation: Fredrik Norland Hagen, 'Et nyt tempelarkiv fra Det Nye Rige' ('A new temple archive from the New Kingdom'), Papyrus 38. årgang nr. 1 (2018), pp. 30-33, Dansk Ægyptologisk Selskab. Issue in honour of Lise Manniche. PDF of the full issue: https://daes.dk/wp-content/uploads/2018/08/Papyrus18_1.pdf (article on PDF pages 30-33).
evidence_tier: Scholarly society magazine article by the excavation's own text specialist (Hagen, University of Copenhagen Egyptologist). Not peer-reviewed; a preliminary popular report in Danish with a short bibliography.
access_status: Fully read. Full issue PDF downloaded from daes.dk and the article text extracted and read in full (pp. 30-33, including figure captions and bibliography).

exact_quotes.danish: Siden 2008 har templet (Henkhet-ankh på ægyptisk) været under udgravning af et spansk-ægyptisk hold, ledet af Myriam Alvarez-Seco. Udgravningerne har fokuseret dels på selve templet, dels på de omkringliggende områder uden for murene.
exact_quotes.english_gloss: Since 2008 the temple (Henkhet-ankh in Egyptian) has been under excavation by a Spanish-Egyptian team led by Myriam Alvarez-Seco. The excavations have focused partly on the temple itself and partly on the surrounding areas outside the walls.

exact_quotes.danish: Områderne udenfor murene har aldrig tidligere været udgravet, og her er der nu gjort flere interessante fund. I den nordlige del af muren opdagede man en sideindgang, som førte ud til templets affaldsdynge, hvor man har fundet både ostraka og papyrusfragmenter med hieratiske tekster.
exact_quotes.english_gloss: The areas outside the walls had never been excavated before, and several interesting finds have now been made there. In the northern part of the wall a side entrance was discovered that led out to the temple's rubbish heap, where both ostraca and papyrus fragments with hieratic texts have been found.

exact_quotes.danish: Papyrusarkivet som omtales blev fundet i en affaldsdynge øst for den nordlige sideindgang (markeret med rødt på kortet).
exact_quotes.english_gloss: The papyrus archive discussed was found in a rubbish heap east of the northern side entrance (marked in red on the map).

exact_quotes.danish: Undertegnede begyndte at arbejde med dette materiale i 2016, og de foreløbige resultater viser, at de fleste af teksterne stammer fra templets administrative arkiv.
exact_quotes.english_gloss: The present author began working on this material in 2016, and the preliminary results show that most of the texts come from the temple's administrative archive.

exact_quotes.danish: Ikke overraskende findes der også fragmenter af hymner og andre religiøse tekster og mindst én kopi af Det Daglige Tempelritual, skrevet i kolonner med kursiv-hieroglyffer. Sidstnævnte er specielt interessant, fordi de hidtil ældst kendte papyruskopier af denne tekst stammer fra det 22. dynasti, dvs. flere hundrede år senere.
exact_quotes.english_gloss: Not surprisingly there are also fragments of hymns and other religious texts, and at least one copy of the Daily Temple Ritual, written in columns in cursive hieroglyphs. The latter is especially interesting because the oldest papyrus copies of this text known until now date to the 22nd Dynasty, i.e. several hundred years later.

exact_quotes.danish: Ligesom det er tilfældet med det administrative materiale, er dette første gang, der er fundet kultiske tekster i et tempel fra det Nye Rige, og de kaster nyt lys over de ritualer, som blev udført til daglig af templets præster. Et godt eksempel herpå er et ritual mod Apophis, der er kendt fra en ritualhåndbog fra Ptolemæertiden (Papyrus Bremner-Rhind).
exact_quotes.english_gloss: As with the administrative material, this is the first time cultic texts have been found in a New Kingdom temple, and they shed new light on the rituals performed daily by the temple's priests. A good example is a ritual against Apophis, known from a ritual handbook of the Ptolemaic period (Papyrus Bremner-Rhind).

exact_quotes.danish: Ritualet, som beskrives i den sene papyrus, inkluderer anvisning på at tage et stykke ubrugt papyrus, tegne en figur af Apophis på denne med rødt blæk, skrive hans navn på papyrussen, og dernæst brænde denne som en del af ritualet – alt imens man fremsiger diverse besværgelser.
exact_quotes.english_gloss: The ritual described in the late papyrus includes instructions to take a piece of unused papyrus, draw a figure of Apophis on it in red ink, write his name on the papyrus, and then burn it as part of the ritual, all while reciting various spells.

exact_quotes.danish: Det siger sig selv, at denne type rituel handling normalt ikke efterlader sig særlig mange arkæologiske spor, så det er usikkert, hvorvidt udførelsen af ritualet var almindelig praksis i ægyptiske templer, og i så tilfælde hvor langt tilbage i tid.
exact_quotes.english_gloss: It goes without saying that this type of ritual act does not normally leave many archaeological traces, so it is uncertain whether performing the ritual was common practice in Egyptian temples, and if so, how far back in time.

exact_quotes.danish: Materialet fra templet inkluderer, utroligt nok, en håndfuld fragmenter af teksten til dette ritual, hvad der viser, at traditionen i hvert fald går tilbage til Thutmose III's tid, dvs. ca. 1000 år tidligere end den kendte ritualhåndbog.
exact_quotes.english_gloss: The material from the temple includes, remarkably, a handful of fragments of the text of this ritual, which shows that the tradition goes back at least to the time of Thutmose III, i.e. about 1000 years earlier than the known ritual handbook.

exact_quotes.danish: Et papyrusfragment med en tegning af Apophis i slangeform, og med hans navn i hieratisk, brugt i et forbandelsesritual i templet. Nederst samme billede efter bearbejdelse i computerprogrammet DStretch for at fremhæve det røde blæk.
exact_quotes.english_gloss: A papyrus fragment with a drawing of Apophis in serpent form, with his name in hieratic, used in a cursing ritual in the temple. Below, the same image after processing in the DStretch software to bring out the red ink.

exact_quotes.danish: Første skridt i et projekt som dette er naturligvis at publicere teksterne.
exact_quotes.english_gloss: The first step in a project like this is of course to publish the texts.

date_and_recency: Published 2018 (Papyrus vol. 38 no. 1; PDF uploaded August 2018). Material discussed: mid-18th Dynasty, reign of Thutmose III (c. 1479-1425 BCE by conventional chronology; the article itself gives no absolute dates), with a later Ramesside (Ramesses II) building phase on site. Hagen began work on the texts in 2016; excavation since 2008.
key_claims: The mortuary temple of Thutmose III (Egyptian Henkhet-ankh) on the Theban west bank, slightly north of the Ramesseum, has been excavated since 2008 by a Spanish-Egyptian team led by Myriam Seco Álvarez (spelled 'Alvarez-Seco' in the article text, 'Seco Álvarez' in the bibliography). Earlier work: Daressy 1888-9, Weigall 1905, Ricke 1934-38.

The areas outside the temple walls had never been excavated. A side entrance in the northern part of the wall led to the temple's rubbish heap, where ostraca and papyrus fragments with hieratic texts were found (Fig. 2 caption: heap east of the northern side entrance).

Most texts come from the temple's administrative archive, chiefly the temple journal (dated entries in red ink, lists of offering deliveries, often from Karnak, and festivals including Thutmose III's coronation feast on I Shemu 3).
This is the first temple archive from a New Kingdom temple; earlier comparanda are Abusir (Old Kingdom), Lahun (Middle Kingdom) and Tebtunis and Edfu (Graeco-Roman). Hagen calls it a 'missing link'.
Literary ostraca (Teaching of Khety, Teaching of Amenemhat, Hymn to the Nile, A Man's Teaching for his Son, Kemit) reflect the mid-18th Dynasty school canon.
At least one copy of the Daily Temple Ritual, in columns of cursive hieroglyphs, was found; previously the oldest known papyrus copies dated to the 22nd Dynasty, several hundred years later.
This is the first time cultic texts have been found in a New Kingdom temple, and they shed light on rituals performed daily by the temple's priests.

A handful of fragments carry the text of a ritual against Apophis known from the Ptolemaic Papyrus Bremner-Rhind (draw Apophis in red ink on unused papyrus, write his name, burn it while reciting spells). This shows the tradition goes back at least to Thutmose III, about 1000 years earlier than the handbook.
Fig. 4-5 show a papyrus fragment with Apophis drawn as a serpent and his name in hieratic, in red ink, described as used in a cursing ritual in the temple.
headline_figures: 'i 2016': year Hagen began working on the texts.
'1888-9' Daressy; '1905' Weigall; '1934-38' Ricke: earlier excavation campaigns.
'ca. 7-8 meter': height difference across the temple's three terraces.
'otte huller til træer ... op til 9 meters dybde': eight tree pits at the entrance, dug down to groundwater up to 9 m deep (persea roots found).
'år 22 af sin regeringstid': Thutmose III held a victory festival here in regnal year 22.
'første måned af Shomu, tredje dag': coronation feast at Thebes on I Shemu 3, one day earlier than the Buto stele's day 4.
'mindst én kopi' (at least one copy) of the Daily Temple Ritual.
'det 22. dynasti, dvs. flere hundrede år senere': previous oldest papyrus copies of the Daily Temple Ritual, 22nd Dynasty, several hundred years later.
'en håndfuld fragmenter' (a handful of fragments) of the Apophis ritual text.
'ca. 1000 år tidligere end den kendte ritualhåndbog': about 1000 years earlier than Papyrus Bremner-Rhind.
dating_and_context: Found in the temple's rubbish heap outside the northern wall, reached by a side entrance in the north wall; the Fig. 2 caption places the heap east of the northern side entrance. Dated by association with the temple of Thutmose III (mid-18th Dynasty). The article does not discuss stratigraphy or give a palaeographic dating argument for individual fragments; Hagen dates the tradition to 'Thutmose III's time'. There is also a Ramesside phase on site (Ramesses II building complex, high priest Khonsu son of Neferhotep, TT 31), so not all material on site is Thutmoside, though the article attributes the archive to the Thutmose III temple. Exact fragment dating within the temple's lifespan: [uncertain].
what_it_says_about_apophis: Very little about the myth itself. Apophis is the target of a ritual 'mod Apophis' (against Apophis) and the fragment is called part of a 'forbandelsesritual' (cursing ritual). Hagen does not discuss the sun's night journey or whether chaos is finally defeated. (Elsewhere in the same issue, Rune Nyord's article mentions the fight against the serpent Apophis that threatens the sun's course, but that is not Hagen's article.)
ritual_practice: Per Papyrus Bremner-Rhind as summarised by Hagen: take a piece of unused papyrus, draw a figure of Apophis on it in red ink, write his name on it, then burn it while reciting spells. Performed by the temple's priests, in the temple. The Thutmose III fragments include the ritual's text and at least one drawing of Apophis as a serpent with his name in hieratic in red ink (Fig. 4-5). Wax figures and piercing are not mentioned. Hagen does not say whether the surviving drawn fragment escaped burning or was a template; the fact that drawn fragments survive in a rubbish heap is not discussed. [uncertain] on that point.
prescribed_vs_attested_frequency: Hagen gives no prescribed frequency for the Apophis ritual. He frames the cultic texts generally as shedding light on rituals 'udført til daglig' (performed daily) by the priests, with the Apophis ritual as 'a good example', but this does not state that the Apophis ritual itself was daily. On attestation he is explicit that the act leaves few archaeological traces, so whether it was common temple practice, and since when, was uncertain; the fragments prove only that the tradition existed by Thutmose III's reign. No count of performances can be inferred. Any 'daily' reading of the Apophis rite specifically from this article would be an overstatement.
relevance_to_angle: Supports the maintenance reading moderately: the Apophis rite sits in the same priestly rubbish as the Daily Temple Ritual and offering journals, i.e. inside the routine paperwork of a working temple, and the tradition is pushed back about 1000 years before Bremner-Rhind. It complicates it in that Hagen does not state the rite's frequency and stresses how little trace such acts leave, so the 'routine' claim must rest on other sources (e.g. Bremner-Rhind's own prescriptions).
limitations_stated: Hagen calls the results 'foreløbige' (preliminary) and the archive 'meget fragmentarisk' (very fragmentary). Key caveat (p. 32): 'denne type rituel handling normalt ikke efterlader sig særlig mange arkæologiske spor, så det er usikkert, hvorvidt udførelsen af ritualet var almindelig praksis i ægyptiske templer' (this kind of ritual act does not normally leave many archaeological traces, so it is uncertain whether performing the ritual was common practice in Egyptian temples). Texts not yet published: 'Første skridt ... er naturligvis at publicere teksterne.' He also notes official offering lists are 'muligvis ideelle' (possibly idealised) compared with administrative practice.
source_discrepancies: Director's name appears as 'Myriam Alvarez-Seco' in the text but 'M. Seco Álvarez' in the bibliography (the usual form is Myriam Seco Álvarez). Temple name spelled 'Henkhet-ankh' in text, 'Henket-ankh' in bibliography. 'Thutmose' and 'Tuthmose' both used. Location wording: text says the north-wall side entrance led to the rubbish heap; Fig. 2 caption says the heap lies east of the northern side entrance; Fig. 1 caption says to the right of that exit. Whether this article is the first published report of the Apophis fragments is not stated by Hagen and was not verified here [uncertain]; it is at least a 2018 early report. 'At least one copy' of the Daily Temple Ritual should not be rounded up to 'copies'.
verification_status: Checked against the primary source opened (full PDF text, pp. 30-33): excavation since 2008 under Seco Álvarez; rubbish heap reached via a north-wall side entrance outside the walls; Hagen working since 2016; at least one Daily Temple Ritual copy, earlier than the previous 22nd Dynasty oldest; first cultic texts from a New Kingdom temple; a handful of Apophis-ritual fragments, c. 1000 years before Bremner-Rhind; the 'few archaeological traces' caveat; Fig. 4-5 red-ink serpent drawing. Not verified: that this is the first report of the Apophis fragments [uncertain]; absolute dates for Thutmose III (not in article); Bremner-Rhind's own wording (only Hagen's summary was read here) [uncertain].
